<explanation>
Below is guidance on drawing a precise system-architecture diagram for the nats.go client library. This is a Go client library (not a full-stack app) that provides core NATS protocol support, higher-level JetStream and Microservice APIs, and pluggable encoding layers. Your diagram will reflect the library’s internal modules, how they relate to one another, and how they interact with external NATS server clusters.

1. Identify the main components  
   - Client Application (your Go code)  
   - Connection Manager & Protocol Engine  
   - Message Parser (internal/parser)  
   - Encoder Layer (encoders/* for JSON, Protobuf, Gob, etc.)  
   - Core NATS API (nats.go: nats.Connect, Publish, Subscribe, Request/Reply)  
   - JetStream API (jetstream/*)  
   - Microservice API (micro/*)  
   - Utilities (context.go, util/tls.go, timer.go, syncx, etc.)  
   - Test Harness & Examples (test/, examples/, bench/)  
   - External NATS Server Cluster  

2. Show relationships & data flows  
   a. Client Application invokes Core NATS API → Connection Manager  
   b. Connection Manager opens TCP/TLS socket to NATS Server(s)  
   c. Incoming/outgoing byte streams pass through Parser and Encoder layers:  
      • Outgoing: Go struct → Encoder → []byte → Protocol Engine → Network  
      • Incoming: Network → Protocol Engine → []byte → Parser → Decoder → Go struct  
   d. JetStream and Microservice APIs sit on top of Core API:  
      • JetStream.New(nc) → uses Core Publish/Subscribe under the covers + admin calls  
      • Micro.NewService(nc) → uses Core API for request/response patterns  
   e. Utilities (context support, timer, syncx) are invoked throughout for timeouts, synchronization, TLS credentials, etc.  
   f. Tests & Examples illustrate all flows—from Core to JetStream to Micro.  

3. Highlight architectural patterns  
   - Layered design:  
     • Bottom: Network Protocol & Connection Manager  
     • Middle: Parser/Encoder abstraction  
     • Top: Public APIs (Core, JetStream, Micro)  
   - Pluggable Encoder/Decoder strategy (Strategy pattern)  
   - Facade pattern for JetStream and Microservice sub-APIs  
   - Use of contexts for cancellations/timeouts (Go idiomatic)  
   - Separation of concerns: internal/ vs. public packages  

4. Tailor diagram to a client-library project  
   - No “frontend” vs. “backend”—rather: “Library User” vs. “NATS Server”  
   - Emphasize extension points (encoders, plugins) and how to add new codecs  
   - Show how JetStream and Microservice modules delegate to core  

5. Diagram elements to include  
   - Boxes (or colored swimlanes) for each major module:  
     • Core Connection & Protocol Engine (color A)  
     • Parser / Encoder Layer (color B)  
     • JetStream API (color C)  
     • Microservice API (color D)  
     • Utilities & Internal Helpers (gray)  
     • Test & Example Suites (dashed border)  
     • External Systems (NATS Server cluster)  
   - Directional arrows for data flow and API calls (label “Publish”, “Subscribe”, “Request”, “ParseFrame”, etc.)  
   - Clear labels: package names (e.g., “internal/parser”, “encoders/json_enc.go”)  
   - Legend or color key to distinguish component types  

6. Step-by-step to drawing  
   1. Draw the External NATS Server cluster on the right.  
   2. On the left, draw your “Library User” box calling into Core API.  
   3. Under Core API, draw Connection Manager → Protocol Engine → network arrows to NATS Server.  
   4. Overlay the Parser and Encoder layers around the Protocol Engine, showing wrap/unwrap.  
   5. Above Core API, place JetStream and Microservice boxes with arrows downward indicating they invoke core methods.  
   6. Off to the side, group internal and util packages your Core and sub-APIs depend on.  
   7. At the bottom, show Test/Example suites invoking various APIs.  

By following this structure you’ll capture all critical modules, their interactions, and extension points—yielding a detailed architecture diagram tailored for nats.go.
